Formation rules: one-syllable adjectives add -er/-est (tall-taller-tallest); spelling rules apply (big-bigger, nice-nicer, happy-happier); longer adjectives use more/most (more interesting, most expensive); irregular forms exist (good-better-best, bad-worse-worst, far-farther/further). Usage rules: comparatives are followed by 'than' (Josh is taller than his sister); much/a lot/far strengthen comparatives; superlatives take 'the' and can be followed by prepositional phrases (the tallest of/in). tasks.task: Search for guidelines on using indirect speech in English, with examples of how to change direct speech to indirect speech, on the Cambridge Dictionary.
tasks.answer: Found the Cambridge Dictionary Grammar guidelines on indirect speech at https://dictionary.cambridge.org/grammar/british-grammar/reported-speech-indirect-speech (article 'Reported speech: indirect speech'). Guidelines: indirect speech focuses more on the content of what someone said rather than their exact words; the structure of the reported clause depends on whether the speaker is reporting a statement, a question or a command. Examples of changing direct speech to indirect speech: statement: '‘I’m tired,’ I said.' → 'I told them (that) I was tired.' (that-clause); question: '‘Are you ready?’ the nurse asked Joel.' → 'The nurse asked Joel if/whether he was ready.' (if/whether-clause), '‘Who are you?’ she asked.' → 'She asked me who I was.' (wh-clause); command: '‘Leave at once!’ they ordered.' → 'They ordered us to leave at once.' (to-infinitive clause). 'That' is often omitted in informal situations.

tasks.task: Use Cambridge Dictionary to understand the use of articles ('a', 'an', 'the') in English Grammar, including examples of usage with both countable and uncountable nouns.
tasks.answer: Final Response: Using the Cambridge Dictionary British Grammar "A/an and the" page (https://dictionary.cambridge.org/grammar/british-grammar/articles): Articles define a noun as specific or unspecific. (1) a/an is the indefinite article: it refers to something mentioned for the first time or to any member of a class, and is used only with singular countable nouns, e.g. "I have a sister and a brother", "That was an excellent meal". (2) the is the definite article: it is used when the reader/listener knows which thing is meant; it can be used with singular and plural countable nouns ("The lion roared", "The lions roared") and with uncountable nouns when they refer to a specific example ("The rice we bought in the Thai shop is much better than the supermarket rice"). (3) We do not use a/an before uncountable nouns: "Could I have rice instead of potatoes with my fish?" (Not: "Could I have a rice"); "I hope we have nice weather" (Not: "I hope we have a nice weather").
